chapter: Dallas bands, Ray Charles and family
title: Teaching Sammy Price piano; subbing at the Savoy
summary: Smith taught dancer Sammy Price blues chords in 1924, and in New York was hired as a dependable pianist for small bands.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Yeah, that's right. I'll tell you somebody else who was a dancer. Sammy Price.
Yeah, the piano player. Sammy Price. In 1924 they was dancing around here, all of them down at Sister(?) (?)
down there, and I learned Sammy Price how to play piano.

Yeah, I learned him. He said, 'Buster, I want to learn how to play piano? Can I come over?' I said, 'Well, come on out there. You go out to somebody's house, and I'll show you a few chords.' Nothin' but the blues.
And you already were able to play the piano then?

Yeah. I always did fool around with the piano. But I wasn't making no habit, takin' no jobs. But when I was in New York, when we wasn't working with Horsecollar, and all them bands come in there, those little old small bands at the Savoy Ballroom, and they needed a piano player, and they'd come and get me. I said, 'Man, there are all these good piano players!' 'Yeah, but you can't depend on 'em. If they ain't drunk, they're full of that old dope or something or another, and they won't make time, and if they come here and somebody gives them a drink, they get drunk, and then we have to carry them away. We can depend on you, because you're a clean-cut man and you're going to be here.' They said, 'We don't want to hear all that much piano playing nohow. So you all right. You fit in the band.' So guys

would send them piano players they would squawk(?) about. "But man, you're goin' up there takin' all the piano players' jobs. They'll have the union put a fine on you about goin' up there playing. Yeah, sure did.
